serenity-nvidia-openai-250b-ohio-backsto:
Nvidia is in talks to guarantee $250 billion of the financing for OpenAI's Ohio data center, the Wall Street Journal reported on July 26. The project's total cost could reach $500 billion, making it the largest single data center project announced so far. Serenity, an X account tracking chip and AI markets, summarized the report.

## What's actually being built in Ohio
SoftBank's energy unit, SB Energy, is developing a 10-gigawatt data center campus in southern Ohio, roughly the output of five or six nuclear reactors combined. OpenAI would sign a long-term lease on the facility, while Nvidia would guarantee $250 billion of the construction financing.

## Why a guarantee carries so much weight
A backstop means that if OpenAI can't repay, Nvidia steps in instead. For banks and bondholders, lending against OpenAI alone, a company that has never turned a profit, is far riskier than lending with the world's largest chipmaker standing behind it. That backing lets far more money get raised at far lower interest rates.

## Where the circular financing complaint comes from
Serenity flagged the same report with a caveat: OpenAI is separately discussing a deal to buy up to $350 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Put together, Nvidia would guarantee $250 billion of OpenAI's debt while trying to sell $350 billion of its own chips into the data center that debt builds. Investor Michael Burry reacted with a short line: "Around and around we go. Nvidia to guarantee $200 billion of ChatGPT's spending on $NVDA chips." He had reportedly just added to his Nvidia short position before posting it.

@@CMP@@The skeptical read|Nvidia is financing demand for its own products, which makes the revenue growth look weaker than it seems, and leaves Nvidia holding the guarantee if OpenAI stumbles|The bullish read|AI data center demand is large and certain enough that this guarantee is a manageable risk against Nvidia's own cash generation

Tech commentator Ed Zitron went further, calling it "insane on so many levels" and "about as bearish as it gets," and questioned why SoftBank is involved at all and where the actual cash is supposed to come from. None of this is confirmed yet; both companies are still described as being in talks.
serenity-cxmt-ipo-star-market-surge:
China's DRAM maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) surged 472% on its trading debut on Shanghai's STAR Market on July 27. Its market cap jumped from $85.5 billion to $489 billion in a single day. Market watchers, including the X account Serenity, reacted with disbelief to what was Asia's biggest IPO of the year.

## How unusual was this listing
CXMT priced its IPO at 8.66 yuan and closed its first day at 49.50 yuan. It raised up to 66.6 billion yuan, beating the previous STAR Market record set by chipmaker SMIC in 2020 (53.2 billion yuan). Reports say the surge pushed CXMT's market cap past Intel's, making it China's largest listed company by that measure.

## Why did money pile in this hard
Demand for AI server DRAM is running well ahead of supply, and that's lifted every memory maker's valuation. According to chip analyst Jukan, Nomura initiated coverage on listing day with a price target of 116 yuan and a 20x P/E multiple, twice Micron's valuation. If that target holds, CXMT's stock would be 13.4 times its IPO price and its market cap would reach 7.76 trillion yuan. Jukan's own reaction: "This is insane."

jukan-skhynix-kioxia-stake-windfall-q2:
Korea's Meritz Securities estimates SK Hynix's Q2 (April-June 2026) pretax profit at around ₩100 trillion, with ₩41.6 trillion of that coming from non-operating gains rather than chip sales. Chip analyst Jukan relayed the estimate on July 27.

## Where does this much money come from
In 2018, SK Hynix invested a combined ₩3.9 trillion through a special purpose company (SPC) alongside Bain Capital's acquisition of Toshiba Memory, now Kioxia. Now that Bain Capital has sold out its entire Kioxia stake, Meritz estimates SK Hynix's SPC1 holding was liquidated along with it, cashing out an eight-year-old investment in one shot.

## How much has it actually grown

## Why the headline number needs a second look
When Bain Capital acquired Toshiba Memory in 2018, the company was up for sale cheap amid an accounting scandal. The money SK Hynix put in back then has multiplied dozens of times over, riding the DRAM supercycle. But none of that came from making or selling more memory. meru-samsung-skhynix-leverage-etf-decay:
It moves twice as fast in both directions, but even sideways trading quietly erodes the principal, according to a breakdown by Korean market commentator Meru of the single-stock 2x leveraged ETFs on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix that listed on May 27, 2026. The headline management fee is a modest 0.29% a year. The real annual cost of holding, once every drag is added up, comes to roughly 14% for the Samsung 2x product and 33% for the SK Hynix 2x product.

## How the principal actually erodes
A 2x ETF adds exposure equal to the investor's capital. Put in 10 million won, and the fund manager layers on another 10 million won of exposure, mostly through futures, for a combined 20 million won riding on the underlying stock. That's what lets the fund return 2% for every 1% move in the stock.

That extra exposure isn't free. Take the Bank of Korea's policy rate (2.75%), subtract the stock's dividend yield, add a 0.5 to 1.5 percentage point premium that shows up when futures get expensive from heavy leveraged demand, then add the 0.29% fee. Samsung's 2x product costs about 2% a year to carry this way, SK Hynix's about 3.5%, higher mainly because its dividend yield is lower, leaving less to subtract.

There's a second, bigger cost: volatility drag. Leveraged ETFs reset to exactly 2x exposure every day after the close. The problem shows up after a loss. Say the underlying falls 10%, from 100 to 90, then rises 11.1% the next day, back to 100, exactly where it started. The 2x product falls 20%, to 80, then rises 22.2% (twice 11.1%), landing at 97.78. The stock is flat. The leveraged version is down 2.2%.

@@CMP@@Common assumption|A leveraged ETF eventually recovers once the underlying moves back to where it started|Meru's math|Daily rebalancing erodes principal continuously even when the underlying just oscillates with no net move

That drag scales with volatility, roughly as its square, Meru estimates. Samsung's volatility runs around 35%, squaring to about 12%. SK Hynix runs hotter, around 55%, squaring to about 30%. Add those to the base carrying cost and the totals land at roughly 14% a year for Samsung's 2x product, 33% for SK Hynix's.

The structure resembles a casino: the house profits not from any single bet, but from running the table and collecting a cut. The manager collects its 0.29% fee steadily, while long-term holders risk losing principal to volatility drag regardless of direction. In a steady uptrend, compounding can push 2x returns above 2x the underlying. Meru's point: in a choppy, directionless market, especially for a stock as volatile as SK Hynix, these products can visibly eat into principal within days.
serenity-substrate-ddr5-wf6-squeeze:
Three different layers of the AI server supply chain tightened at once this week: substrates, memory modules and a specialty gas. Serenity, an X account that tracks chip and AI markets, rounded up the signals on July 26.

## What's tightening at the same time
Samsung Electronics is reportedly struggling to secure large FC-BGA substrates, the advanced packaging layer built on ABF substrate technology that connects a high-end chip to its board. Ibiden (4062), one of its suppliers, reportedly asked for long-term agreement (LTA) guarantees, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics asked for prepayment. Normally suppliers chase customers. Here, the supplier is setting the terms.

Memory looks similar. 64GB DDR5 server memory modules have jumped 146% versus end-June contract pricing.

## The gas squeeze nobody's watching
Spot prices for tungsten hexafluoride, or WF6, are up 2.1 to 2.5 times year over year. WF6 is the gas used to etch tungsten wiring into semiconductor wafers. If this gas runs short, the wiring step can bottleneck even when finished chips are abundant. Japan's Kanto Denka and Chuo Gas have both announced permanent production halts, and 3M is exiting PFAS (fluorinated compound) production altogether, leaving a supply gap.

A supply-chain map Stacks covered earlier argued the real AI hardware bottleneck isn't the flashy GPU, it's the unglamorous layers underneath, substrates and components. These three data points look like that map's warning showing up in real time.

One caveat: many of these components serve both general-purpose and AI-datacenter demand, so not every bit of tightness here is purely an AI story. Still, three separate layers needed to finish a single server tightening at once is worth watching.
kobeissi-sp500-margin-record-q2-2026:
S&P 500 companies are on track to post a 15.7% net profit margin for the second quarter of 2026, the highest reading since the data series began in 2009.

If the figure holds once every company has reported, it would mark the tenth consecutive quarter of rising margins. So far, 27% of S&P 500 companies have posted second-quarter results, and among them 86% beat earnings-per-share estimates while 80% beat revenue estimates.

## Why did margins climb this much
Alphabet, Google's parent company, is the single biggest contributor to the margin gain after beating earnings forecasts by a wide margin. The Kobeissi Letter, which tracks the data, summed up the broader pattern as AI driving historic earnings growth.

Net profit margin is what's left of revenue after every cost is subtracted, including cost of goods, wages, interest and taxes. A rising margin means a company is keeping more out of every dollar it brings in, even if revenue itself doesn't grow as fast.

Read next to a card Stacks covered earlier, though, the picture gets more complicated. That card tracked labor's share of national income falling to a record low. Corporate margins climbing to a record high while labor's cut of the pie shrinks are two sides of the same coin: part of this margin expansion comes from new AI-driven revenue, and part of it comes from how hard companies have squeezed costs, including labor costs.

One caveat matters here. The 15.7% figure reflects only 27% of S&P 500 companies that have reported so far. The rest, including Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Amazon, which report this week, still need to weigh in before the number is final. It could hold, or it could come down.
meru-rescene-themuse-funding-rounds:
A tiny K-pop label with 10 million won ($7,000) in starting capital just walked through every stage of Korean startup fundraising, seed, Pre-Series A, Series A, in real time. Market commentator Meru used the girl group RESCENE and its agency, The Muse, to show how the funding ladder actually works.

## How do startups actually raise money in stages
Startup funding in Korea typically climbs from seed, to Pre-Series A, to Series A, to Series B. Seed money comes in when a company has little more than a prototype or an idea. Pre-Series A is the next round, raised to test whether that prototype actually works in the market, typically hundreds of millions to a billion won in Korea.

The Muse was founded in Jeju in December 2020 by three Berklee College of Music alumni, with just 10 million won in capital. In May 2023 it raised its Pre-Series A, under 1 billion won from Smartstudy Ventures and By4M Studio, and used the money to train a five-member girl group. RESCENE, with an average age of 16.6, debuted in March 2024.

What came next was harder. None of the group's early albums produced visible traction, in sales or YouTube views. In the second half of 2025, The Muse went after a 5 billion won Series A for a new album and operating costs, but by June 2026 it had raised only 2 billion won, from JB Investment, K-Net Investment Partners and earlier Pre-A backers.

## Why the fundraising suddenly stopped
The turn came in May 2026. A personal video from RESCENE's leader Wonyi went viral, pulling older songs back into circulation with it. More than 100 ad inquiries poured in. Rather than keep raising, The Muse closed its Series A at 2 billion won, planning to build a higher valuation before attempting Series B.

The numbers show why the stakes are high. 2025 revenue came to 1.77 billion won with a 5.69 billion won operating loss, worse on both counts than 2024's 2.1 billion won in revenue and 200 million won loss. The company's only revenue source is a single group.

Meru calls this one-team risk: with no second act in the portfolio, anything that happens to RESCENE shakes the whole company. He points to HYBE, which started as a single-artist bet on BTS before acquiring labels like Source Music and Pledis to diversify, as a model worth studying, adding that The Muse should copy HYBE's strengths, not just imitate it wholesale.
doomberg-natgas-demand-shortage-2028:
The US could face a demand-driven natural gas shortage starting in 2028, with working storage potentially running out by 2030, according to a widely read energy newsletter.

Matthew Smith, who runs investment firm Chronometer Partners, laid out the case in a recent letter, and Doomberg reviewed it and added its own take.

Natural gas is the same fuel that heats stoves and furnaces in millions of homes, and it's also the single largest fuel burned to generate US electricity.
Domestic shale gas production has more than doubled over the past 15 years, to over 100 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d), and Smith doesn't dispute that growth.

## Why demand, not supply, is the problem

His concern lies elsewhere.
Much of the power AI data centers consume ultimately comes from gas-fired plants.
If data center buildout keeps accelerating faster than gas production can scale, supply eventually falls behind demand.
Smith puts that turning point at 2028, and says storage could run dry by 2030 if the trend holds.

Doomberg has historically been skeptical of "the US is about to run out of gas" narratives, pointing to a long history of ever-rising shale output despite rock-bottom prices.
Even so, the newsletter said it found much to agree with in Smith's letter, and only a few points worth doubting, though which specific points remain behind its paywall.

jukan-meta-storage-gpu-hour-economics:
Chip-industry commentator Jukan relayed his own reading of a Meta Engineering blog post, arguing that the metric for choosing AI data center storage is shifting from dollars-per-terabyte to dollars-per-GPU-hour.
Meta published the storage design philosophy on its engineering blog, and a few hours later Jukan noted that Micron had also put out a related white paper with Meta.

AI compute chips like Nvidia's GPUs roughly triple in processing speed every two years, but the storage and networking gear that feeds them data hasn't kept pace.
When a GPU can't get its data fast enough, an expensive chip sits idle.
Meta describes this as one of the biggest single causes of wasted GPU time in AI infrastructure.

## Why the storage yardstick is changing

Storage has traditionally been judged on how cheaply it can hold a terabyte of data, the dollars-per-terabyte metric.
But in AI training, if slow storage leaves GPUs idle longer, that lost compute time can cost more than whatever was saved on storage.
So Meta's engineering team argues storage should instead be valued by how well it keeps GPUs busy, a dollars-per-GPU-hour metric.

A factory comparison makes this concrete.
Skimping on a cheap part that ends up stalling the entire assembly line costs far more than the part itself was worth.
An hour of GPU time costs far more than whatever gets saved by buying cheaper storage, which is why the math flips.

If this yardstick becomes an industry standard, makers of fast, high-performance NAND flash, the kind of chip that keeps data even when the power is off, gain an easier case for charging more for storage that keeps GPUs fed.
The competitive center of gravity shifts from raw capacity to raw speed.
The fact that Micron co-published this framing with Meta itself signals that storage vendors are starting to use it as a marketing argument too.
macro-week-2026-07-26:
Four numbers landed within days of each other this week, and they pull in different directions at once. China's central bank pumped $118.1 billion combined into its banking system through medium-term loans and reverse repos, the most since February, right after weak growth data. Chinese buyers imported 173 tonnes of gold in June, the most in a single month since March 2024. Meanwhile in the United States, investors pulled $7.1 billion out of investment-grade corporate bond funds in a week, the fastest outflow since the pandemic. And globally, emerging-market carry trades, borrowing in euros to chase yield in currencies like the Brazilian real and Turkish lira, are up 18% this year, their best start since 2005.

Read side by side, these don't tell one story, they tell two that pull against each other. Gold buying and central bank liquidity injections are defensive moves, the kind a government makes when it doesn't fully trust its own growth numbers. Carry trades are the opposite: money chasing yield with borrowed cash, a bet that calm currency markets keep paying out. Sitting in between is the corporate bond outflow, quiet stress in US credit that isn't showing up in stock prices or currency volatility yet.

## How to read four signals pointing in different directions
Put together, the picture is a market that is barbelling risk. Currency traders are leaning further into risk-taking than they have in two decades, while China hedges its own growth doubts with gold and stimulus, and US credit investors quietly step back from corporate debt. None of these four moves cancels out the others, they are happening at the same time, in different corners of the same global market.
meru-china-russia-gas-talks-collapse:
Gas pricing negotiations between Russia and China over the second Power of Siberia pipeline (POS2) have collapsed, and the gap between the two sides is stark: China reportedly offered just $50 per 1,000 cubic meters, while Russia asked for $250, according to Korean market commentator Meru.

The numbers matter because $50 doesn't come close to covering Russia's own delivery cost. Gas from Russia's Yamal fields is estimated to cost around $125 per 1,000 cubic meters to pipe to China, so China's offer sits at well under half of what it would cost Russia just to deliver the gas, let alone turn a profit. By comparison, China currently pays Russia around $259 for gas flowing through the existing Power of Siberia 1 pipeline, Gazprom charges other international buyers an average of around $420, and China's own LNG import price from suppliers like Qatar runs around $370. Russia's $250 ask, in that light, looked like a reasonable middle ground, not an aggressive number.

## Why would China lowball this badly
Meru links the breakdown to an unrelated dispute: a rail bridge over the Tumen River, which separates China from North Korea near where China's territory reaches close to the Sea of Japan. China has long wanted better access to the sea through this route, and has pushed for the bridge, completed in April 2026, to open for larger ship traffic. Russia has been slow to finish the approach roads and customs facilities on its side, and North Korea reportedly suspects Russia is dragging its feet out of deference to China's own sensitivities. Meru's theory is that China's rock-bottom gas offer may be a form of pressure or retaliation tied to that frustration, though he is careful to say the real motive is unknowable from outside.

@@CMP@@Common read|This is just tough commercial negotiating over a long-term energy contract.|Meru's read|The gap is too extreme for pure hardball, and may signal China's displeasure over an unrelated bridge dispute.

The stakes are asymmetric. Russia's pipeline exports to the European Union have shrunk from around 150 billion cubic meters a year before 2022 to under 25 billion, and the EU has committed to ending Russian LNG imports by the end of 2026 and all Russian gas imports by October 2027. That leaves China as Russia's dominant remaining buyer for gas that, unlike LNG, cannot easily be rerouted to another customer once a pipeline is built. China, which can still buy LNG elsewhere at a higher price, has less urgency to close the deal quickly.
jukan-goldman-china-dram-catchup:
Goldman Sachs held an expert call with a Chinese DRAM industry insider, and semiconductor analyst Jukan relayed the key takeaways.
The headline point: Chinese DRAM makers' prices have already caught up to global leaders like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron.

"Yield" is the share of chips on a wafer that come out working. A lower yield means more defective chips get scrapped, so producing the same volume costs more.
According to the call, Chinese suppliers' yields are still likely below the leaders', yet their prices haven't budged lower to compensate.

Charging leader-level prices while carrying higher production costs points to one of two things: Chinese makers are eating the loss to defend market share, or state subsidies are covering the gap.
Either way, it suggests global DRAM pricing power isn't sitting exclusively with the incumbent leaders the way it used to.

The call also touched on the technology roadmap.
Chinese DRAM makers are expected to make further progress on 3D-stacked DRAM in 2027, and capacity expansions underway in Hefei, Shanghai, and Beijing are slated to be fully operational by 2028.
Some fabs reportedly run mostly on domestically produced Chinese equipment, with one notable exception: high-end lithography tools, the machines that etch circuit patterns onto wafers.

That exception explains why US export controls on China's chip industry have zeroed in specifically on lithography equipment.
The rest of the toolchain is already being replaced with domestic gear, so the underlying bet is that blocking lithography alone can still slow China's push for DRAM self-sufficiency.
How much longer that bet holds is the thing to watch next.
jukan-huawei-ai-chip-shipments-double:
Huawei is on track to ship around 1.5 million of its own AI accelerator chips this year, roughly double the volume it shipped in 2025, according to a Wall Street Journal report relayed by semiconductor analyst Jukan on X. The jump matters because it comes despite years of US export controls designed to cut China off from advanced chipmaking equipment and Nvidia's most powerful GPUs.

Huawei's AI chips, sold under its Ascend brand, are the centerpiece of China's push to build a domestic alternative to Nvidia's dominant AI computing stack. Export controls, first imposed in 2019 and tightened repeatedly since, block Huawei from buying the most advanced lithography tools and from importing Nvidia's top-tier chips into China. The policy bet was that without those tools, Huawei's chip output would stay small and lag years behind the cutting edge.

## Why doubling shipments changes the calculus
A doubling in shipment volume complicates that bet. It does not mean Huawei's chips match Nvidia's newest GPUs in raw performance, Huawei still relies on older manufacturing processes that produce lower yields and less efficient chips per wafer. But volume is its own kind of progress: more chips shipped means more Chinese AI labs and cloud providers can train and run models on domestic hardware instead of waiting for, or working around, Nvidia supply.

@@CMP@@Common read|Export controls have starved China of AI compute, keeping it years behind.|What the numbers show|Huawei's shipments are doubling year over year, even if per-chip performance still lags Nvidia's newest GPUs.

The report doesn't disclose yield rates, chip architecture, or which customers are absorbing the volume, so it's hard to know how much of this capacity goes to frontier model training versus lighter inference work. Still, for investors watching Nvidia's China exposure, and for policymakers debating whether to tighten or ease export rules, the shipment trajectory is one of the clearest signals available of how fast Huawei's alternative stack is actually scaling.
jukan-nand-sandisk-lta-bearish-pushback: Bearish rumors about NAND flash memory have been circulating this week, especially out of China, centered on weak QLC (a lower-cost, higher-density flash type) pricing negotiations. Chip-industry analyst Jukan pushed back on X, arguing the pessimism reads too much into normal contract dynamics. The trigger was reports that SanDisk signed a long-term agreement (LTA) with Meta at roughly $0.38 per unit. SanDisk's opening quote was near $0.50, which is expensive for QLC and close to the price of TLC, a higher-margin flash type. The $0.38 settlement came down from there. Jukan said this is not surprising: SanDisk is the most aggressive NAND maker in locking in LTAs and plans to commit more than half its total volume to them, so it is naturally willing to price below the prevailing quarterly contract rate to secure that volume. He added that Chinese module makers were turned away when they tried to sell more enterprise SSDs to Chinese cloud providers, but that is because those providers already buy directly from YMTC, not because demand is weak. Reports that hyperscalers are pushing back on QLC drive pricing also do not worry him, since he believes neoclouds have enough demand to absorb any leftover volume. With memory stocks selling off, he said the bearish headlines are gaining more traction than they deserve, and he remains bullish on memory.
jukan-cxmt-3d-ic-niche-strategy: The chip industry's race to boost AI performance is shifting from process shrinks to 3D stacking, which fuses logic and memory in one package, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are staying cautious about commercializing it while China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) moves to claim the niche, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports. Samsung's foundry division is reportedly fielding a steady stream of inquiries about 3D ICs as demand grows for custom AI chips like ASICs and inference chips alongside Nvidia's general-purpose GPUs. Industry officials say custom, 3D-stacked DRAM is a fundamentally different business from the standardized, mass-produced DRAM that Samsung and SK hynix are built around, since every customer wants a different memory configuration and stacking method, making it hard to run profitably at scale. That is why the two Korean giants are expected to keep 3D IC work at the research stage rather than mobilizing full business units, while later entrants chasing niche demand move first. CXMT, blocked from the high-bandwidth memory market by US export controls, is reportedly building 3D IC capability instead, and Taiwan's Winbond is named alongside it as another niche player. CXMT has reportedly already produced several 3D DRAM sample chips ahead of rivals worldwide.
kobeissi-margin-debt-net-credit-record: A fresh sign of investors piling into stocks with borrowed money rather than cash has emerged. According to The Kobeissi Letter, net credit balances, the cash investors hold in brokerage accounts minus margin debt (money borrowed against stock holdings), fell $70 billion in June to a record negative $1.06 trillion. A negative reading means investors collectively owe more than they hold in cash. That deficit has more than quadrupled since the 2022 bear market, over which time margin debt itself climbed $895 billion to a record $1.50 trillion. Kobeissi contrasts this with the 2008 financial crisis, when net credit balances stayed positive, meaning investors held more cash than debt amid a broad flight from risk into safety. The current numbers point the opposite way, with Kobeissi describing investor risk appetite as being at unprecedented levels.
jukan-korea-memory-mega-mou-950b: SK hynix agreed to supply $750 billion (about 1,085 trillion won) worth of advanced memory chips to Nvidia and other US tech giants over the next five years, according to Kim Yong-beom, South Korea's presidential chief of staff for policy, relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X. The same day, Samsung Electronics signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Broadcom covering $200 billion (about 290 trillion won) in advanced memory supply and foundry cooperation for AI chip production, also over five years. Both announcements came during President Lee Jae-myung's visit to Silicon Valley, where South Korean officials have been framing the trip as a showcase for the country's memory chip industry. The SK hynix deal spans Nvidia and unnamed other technology companies, while the Samsung-Broadcom MOU pairs memory supply with foundry work, since Broadcom designs custom AI chips for clients like Google and Meta that need a manufacturing partner. Around the same time, Anthropic's chief executive said separately that the company had signed its own supply agreements with both Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, adding a third major AI buyer to the mix. The deals come as demand for memory from AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic has surged all at once, with Samsung and SK hynix each pursuing large customers in the race for high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, market share. The figures are large enough to raise questions about how binding they are. Both are framed as five-year memorandums rather than signed, itemized contracts, so how much of the $950 billion combined total converts into actual revenue depends on terms still being worked out.
jukan-apple-micron-china-memory-lobbying: Apple is lobbying the White House to allow Chinese-made memory chips in its products, according to the Wall Street Journal, as memory prices used in iPhones have surged this year. Micron, the US memory chipmaker, is reportedly pushing back hard, arguing the exemption should never be granted. Chip-industry commentator Jukan, writing on X, disputed Apple's stated reasoning. Apple has argued that rising memory costs are an inflation problem that forces it to raise iPhone prices, but Jukan calculated that a roughly fivefold jump in memory prices added only about $50 to Apple's per-unit cost, while Apple raised iPhone prices by $250, a gap he says undercuts the inflation argument and points instead to margin protection. Jukan also referenced Apple's practice in 2023 of buying NAND flash memory near cost and reselling it to consumers at what he described as a 90% margin, calling the move vicious, and said Micron chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra has held a grudge against Apple dating back to his time as a SanDisk co-founder. The dispute comes as Chinese memory makers YMTC and CXMT have been rapidly gaining NAND and DRAM market share, so if Apple does expand its use of Chinese chips, it could also weaken the pricing power of US memory makers including Micron. Those characterizations and anecdotes are Jukan's own framing rather than independently confirmed reporting, though the underlying WSJ account of the lobbying dispute between Apple and Micron is sourced reporting.
semianalysis-amd-cuda-moat-advancing-ai-: Semiconductor analysis firm SemiAnalysis has upgraded its outlook on AMD's chances of challenging Nvidia's software dominance from a 0% chance in its first critical report to what it now calls a great chance of success, provided AMD clears two remaining risks. The firm's review of AMD's MI455X accelerator, unveiled at Advancing AI 2026, found it is the first datacenter chip built on TSMC's 2-nanometer N2 process and packs 12 stacks of HBM4 memory for 432 gigabytes per package, more than the 8 stacks and 288 gigabytes Nvidia and Google use. Anthropic has committed to deploying 2 gigawatts of AMD chips, and Microsoft, which had dropped AMD after quality problems with an earlier chip, has reversed course and will deploy the new Helios racks, likely for OpenAI as the end customer. SemiAnalysis flagged two risks holding AMD back: a slow production ramp for the Helios rack due to reliability issues in its backplane design, and a chronic shortage of internal GPU clusters for software testing that has left AMD's automated test parity with Nvidia's CUDA behind schedule, with a target originally set for this event now pushed to October. AMD also announced a partnership with Cerebras on disaggregated inference technology meant to speed up response times. Meta ordered a scaled-down version of the MI455 that SemiAnalysis says hurts AMD's chances there, though it reports Meta has since begun reconsidering its infrastructure strategy after the firm's earlier criticism.
meru-treasury-yield-deficit-not-just-oil: Rising oil prices explain only part of the Treasury yield spike, Korean investment blogger Meru argues, the bigger driver is a structural mismatch between how much debt Washington needs to sell and how much the market wants to buy. The 10-year yield broke above 4.7% intraday, and most coverage blames it on crude, since the Strait of Hormuz is blocked again and Houthi attacks threaten the Red Sea. Oil does feed into inflation broadly, through gasoline, plastics, fertilizer and power generation costs, but breakeven inflation, the rate implied by inflation-protected Treasuries, has barely moved, sitting around 2.3% for both 10 and 30-year debt. Instead, the 30-year real yield has climbed to its highest since the 2008 financial crisis, meaning borrowing itself has simply gotten more expensive. Meru traces that to Treasury supply and demand: the market has grown from $4.5 trillion in 2007 to $31 trillion today, China has flipped from buyer to net seller in favor of gold, Japanese investors sold $29.6 billion of Treasuries net in Q1 2026, and the Fed keeps shrinking its balance sheet. Washington's annual interest bill has topped $1.2 trillion, the FY2026 deficit is projected near $2.07 trillion, and a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs forced billions in refunds that analysts say adds roughly $180 billion a year to the deficit through 2036. Big Tech is competing for the same buyers too: global corporate bond issuance hit a record $3.68 trillion in the first half of 2026, led by Amazon's $54 billion, forcing the Treasury to offer richer yields to compete for pension and insurance money.
serenity-aaoi-pluggables-cpo-coexist:
The debate over whether co-packaged optics (CPO) will soon make traditional pluggable optical transceivers obsolete in AI data centers got a reality check this week. Analyst Serenity relayed comments from a photonics-industry CEO, made on an industry podcast called "Market Insights: Photonics & AI," arguing pluggables have roughly another decade of relevant life left, not months.

The exchange started with a reader asking whether Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is in trouble as CPO, which mounts optical modules directly next to a processor's chip package instead of plugging them in at the edge of a server, gains traction. Serenity's answer: not exactly. AAOI is also developing CPO technology, it's simply further behind on commercializing it than some peers, so lagging on one architecture doesn't mean the company is being left out of the market entirely.

## Why CPO doesn't kill pluggables overnight
The CEO's broader framework, as relayed, is that the industry is heading toward multiple coexisting architectures rather than one clean winner. Alongside pluggables and CPO, a newer category called near-package optics (NPO), which sits closer to the chip than a pluggable but doesn't go as far as full co-packaging, is described as a major opportunity over the next five years. That means capital and R&D spending across the optical supply chain is spreading across at least three architectures rather than concentrating on CPO alone.

The binding constraint across all three paths, per the CEO, isn't architecture choice but manufacturing capacity and raw material availability, likely a reference to the industry's tight supply of continuous-wave (CW) lasers used to power optical modules. That suggests demand for optical components is outrunning the industry's ability to build them, regardless of which technology wins.

This is secondhand color from a podcast relayed through a tweet, not a company roadmap or earnings guidance, so it should be read as directional industry sentiment rather than a confirmed timeline for AAOI or any single supplier.
kobeissi-m2-outpaces-gdp-g7: Money creation keeps outpacing real economic growth across the G7, a fresh set of figures shows. According to The Kobeissi Letter, Canada's M2 money supply (a measure of cash, checking deposits and savings-type accounts) has grown 368% since January 2004, the largest increase among G7 economies, while the Canadian economy expanded just 159% in nominal terms over the same period. The US shows a similar gap, with M2 up 279% against 171% nominal GDP growth. France's M2 has surged 258% and the eurozone's 211%, both far outpacing nominal growth of 84% and 102% respectively. Japan is the outlier in the other direction, with M2 up only 90% since 2004, but its economy grew just 25% over that span, the slowest pace in the G7. Kobeissi frames this as a widening gap between how fast money is being created and how fast economies are actually growing.
trump-xi-putin-no-weapons-iran: President Trump said both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin personally assured him they will not sell weapons to Iran, a claim that, if it holds, would cut off two of the countries most capable of arming Tehran as its war grinds into its fifth month. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Xi made the pledge at their recent meeting in Beijing and said it extends to Chinese companies as well, not just the government. He framed the assurance as tied to the broader US-China relationship, saying he is doing Xi "very big favors" in return. On Putin, Trump said the Russian leader made a similar commitment despite the ongoing war in Ukraine, where Russia's relationship with the US continues alongside its ties to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump drew a distinction with his own weapons sales, saying the US sells arms to NATO countries rather than directly to Ukraine, and that what those countries do with the weapons afterward is not something he tracks. He added that any weapons flow from China or Russia to Iran would be "very bad for them," without elaborating on what response that might trigger. The statement comes as Iran has already rejected a US-backed ceasefire proposal from Iraqi mediators, and as oil and shipping routes near the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea remain under pressure from the conflict. Neither Beijing nor Moscow has publicly confirmed Trump's account of the conversations.
jukan-amd-mi500-tam-14t: Semiconductor analyst Jeff Pu has raised his forecast for the AI accelerator market to $1.4 trillion by 2030, up from an earlier $1 trillion estimate, and now expects the market to already reach $1 trillion by 2028, according to a note relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X. Pu's note, focused on AMD's AI roadmap, also lifted the server CPU total addressable market to more than $220 billion by 2030, with agentic AI workloads expected to make up roughly half of that demand and the ratio of CPUs to GPUs in data centers tightening toward 1:1. On AMD's own hardware, Pu highlighted the MI455X accelerator as a major step up from its predecessor, the MI355X, citing 34 times higher throughput and 18 times lower cost per generated token, and said it already beats Nvidia's B200 chip on some large language model inference workloads. Looking further out, Pu said AMD's next-generation MI500 chip will bring optical interconnects, a faster way of linking chips together using light instead of electrical signals, putting it ahead of Nvidia's upcoming Rubin Ultra chip in areas like high-bandwidth memory, four-die packaging, and how many chips can be linked into a single system. He also flagged AMD's Venice server CPU as the strongest option for AI workloads, with 2 to 2.2 times higher throughput than competing chips, and estimated around 300,000 CoWoS advanced packaging units will be built for AMD in 2027, which would lift the average price AMD can charge per chip. Pu kept his price target and estimates unchanged despite the upgraded market forecasts.
